subject: history

moments.title: Vesalius publishes De Humani Corporis Fabrica
moments.body: Vesalius's vast illustrated anatomy textbook is published in Basel, with woodcuts by the workshop of Titian. He corrects around 200 errors in Galen — including showing that the human jaw is one bone, not two. He insists on personal dissection rather than reading authorities.
moments.takeaway: Vesalius was 28 when the Fabrica was published. The break with 1,400-year-old Galenic authority is one of the founding moments of modern science.

moments.title: Harvey's De Motu Cordis
moments.body: Harvey publishes 'An Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals'. Using vivisection and calculation, he shows that blood circulates, pumped by the heart — overturning Galen's idea that blood is produced and consumed.

quote.text: I have been so much affected by the writings of the older anatomists.

moments.takeaway: Harvey calculated that the heart pumps too much blood per minute to be continuously produced. The mathematics killed Galenic physiology.

moments.title: Capillaries observed
moments.body: Malpighi uses the new microscope to observe capillaries in frog lungs — the missing link in Harvey's circulation theory. The full picture of the cardiovascular system is now complete.
moments.takeaway: Harvey, who died in 1657, didn't live to see his theory completed.

now.title: Foundations of physiology
now.body: Harvey's work is the founding text of physiology as a distinct discipline. The framework — quantitative measurement, mechanical models of bodily function — extended to every other system over the following centuries. Stephen Hales (blood pressure, 1733), Marcello Malpighi (microscopic anatomy), Marie François Bichat (tissues, 1800) built on Harvey's approach.
now.open_questions: Why did the scientific revolution happen in 17th-century Europe? The combination of universities, printing, patronage, and a culture of public dispute and experiment is the standard answer. Harvey's training in Padua (where Vesalius and Galileo had worked) is part of the pattern.

reflection: Medicine before 1543 worked from ancient authority. After 1628 it worked from observation and measurement. The shift was led by individuals willing to contradict Galen — and the result was a discipline that could progress, slowly, beyond the limits of antiquity.
